blocks.heading: A token is a mapping
text: Your wallet lists a balance of some token. It feels like the wallet contains it.
The wallet contains a key. The token is a row in a table you do not control.

blocks.heading: The whole standard is six functions
text: EIP-20 does not describe a coin. It describes an interface that a contract must answer to.

blocks.label: EIP-20, in full
blocks.code:
totalSupply()          balanceOf(owner)
transfer(to, value)    transferFrom(from, to, value)
approve(spender, v)    allowance(owner, spender)

blocks.heading: And the state behind it is one line
text: Everything a token _is_ lives in a single mapping inside a single contract.

blocks.alt: Two wallets pointing at one contract that holds a table of addresses and amounts
blocks.caption: Both wallets are reading the same table. Neither contains anything but a key.

blocks.heading: Sending is not moving
text: A transfer is a call to that contract, which subtracts from one row, adds to another, and emits an event.
Nothing travelled. Two numbers changed, in a place neither party owns.

blocks.question: Unfamiliar tokens sometimes appear in a wallet nobody sent them to. Has the wallet been compromised?
answer: No. Anyone can call `transfer` and credit any address, and there is no acceptance step to decline it. The arrival proves nothing about your keys.
The danger is the next step: these are usually bait, and the contract you interact with to "claim" or sell them is the attack. Receiving is harmless; touching it is not.

blocks.heading: The mirror image of that
text: Send tokens to a contract that was never written to handle them, and the table records that contract as the holder.
If it has no code that moves them, nothing ever will. They are not burned - they still count in the supply. They are simply unreachable forever.

blocks.heading: The second mapping
text: Contracts cannot take your tokens without permission, so the standard adds `approve`: you record an allowance, and the spender calls `transferFrom` later.
Two steps, with a gap between them. The gap is public.

blocks.title: The approve race
text: Lower an existing allowance from 100 to 50 and a spender watching the mempool can spend the 100 first, then the 50 after your change lands. 150 from an allowance you were trying to reduce.
The standard itself notes this. The workaround is to set it to zero first - two transactions, two fees, for one change of mind.

blocks.heading: And the habit that makes it worse
text: Approving an unlimited amount once is convenient, and it is what most interfaces ask for by default.
It means a contract that is later compromised or upgraded can take the whole balance, not the amount you were spending that afternoon.
Nothing in EIP-20 forbids privileged functions, and large issued tokens have them: minting, pausing, and address blacklists held by the issuer.
Whether your balance is really yours is a fact about that one contract's code. Not about the standard, and not about the chain underneath it.

blocks.heading: One sentence worth keeping
text: A token is an entry in one contract's table, and "self-custody" only ever meant custody of the key that entry is filed under.
That table is public, and so is every payment in this course. The last chapter is about what that costs.
